examples.knowledge_point: Calculating the Determinant of the Inverse of a Matrix
examples.worked_solution:
Given an invertible $n\times n$ matrix $A,$ we have

$$
|A^{-1}| = \dfrac{1}{|A|}.
$$

First, we find $|A|$ using a Laplace expansion across the $3$rd row:

$$
\begin{aligned}|A| & =|\begin{aligned}2 & 14 & -1 \\ 7 & -6 & -6 \\ 0 & -3 & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =-3(-1)^{3+2}|\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 7 & -6\end{aligned}| \\  & =3\cdot (-12+7) \\  & =-15\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, we obtain 

$$
\det(A^{-1}) =  \dfrac{1}{|A|} = -\dfrac{1}{15}.
$$

feedback.worked_solution:
Given two $n\times n$ matrices $M$ and $N,$ we have

$$
det(MN)=det(M)\cdot det(N).
$$

In our case, this gives

$$
det(P)=det[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & 0 \\ 5 & 1 & 0 \\ -7 & 4 & -2\end{aligned}]\cdot det[\begin{aligned}8 & 6 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & -5 \\ 0 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$

Notice that both matrices are triangular. Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}det(P) & =(3\cdot 1\cdot (-2))\cdot (8\cdot 1\cdot (-1)) \\  & =(-6)\cdot (-8) \\  & =48.\end{aligned}
$$
